titre: Galileo First Mistook Jupiter's Moons for Fixed Stars
accroche: On January 7, 1610, Galileo notes three small stars in a line near Jupiter. It takes him four nights of observation to understand what he has seen.
contenu_vulgarise:
On January 7, 1610, in the first hour of the night, Galileo observes Jupiter through a telescope he has just prepared for himself, more powerful than his previous one. He notices what he had never been able to see: three small stars, tiny but very bright, very close to the planet. They lie along a straight line parallel to the ecliptic, two to the east of Jupiter and one to the west.

Their alignment and brightness intrigue him a little, but he takes them to be among the fixed stars, and he barely notes their distance from the planet.

## Four Nights to Change His Mind

On January 8, he goes back to look at the same region of the sky. The three points are now all to the west of Jupiter, closer to one another and separated by equal intervals. The night before, Jupiter lay to the west of two of them; it is now to the east of all three.

His first explanation is an astronomer's. He fears that Jupiter has moved otherwise than the calculations predict, and has passed these stars by its own motion. He waits impatiently for the next night. The sky is overcast.

On January 10, he sees only two points, both to the east of Jupiter and still on the same line as the planet. He thinks the third is hidden behind it. Two observations make him change course. First, such a pattern of positions cannot possibly be Jupiter's doing. Second, they are always the same stars: no other appears, in front or behind, at a great distance along the zodiac. The exchange of positions therefore belongs to the little stars themselves.

On January 11, he sees only two, to the east. The farther one is almost twice as large as the other, whereas the night before they had seemed equal. Galileo concludes without hesitation that there are three bodies in the sky revolving around Jupiter, as Venus and Mercury revolve around the Sun. On January 13, he sees four at once.

## What the Log Shows

The scene is often summed up like this: Galileo aims a telescope at Jupiter and sees its moons. His own account says otherwise. He saw points of light, first ranked them among the fixed stars, then among the effects of a motion of Jupiter, and gave up both readings one after the other because his records, night after night, could not support them. The discovery owes as much to the log as to the telescope.

He did not keep it to himself. The Sidereus Nuncius appeared in Venice on March 13, 1610, and reproduces the positions recorded night by night, with diagrams. Any reader can therefore retrace the reasoning, and see the initial error before the correction.

Repeating the observation is another matter. Kepler, the first astronomer to publicly support Galileo's results in April 1610, does not publish his own confirmation until August, for lack of sufficiently powerful telescopes.

repere.texte: Galileo observes Jupiter on January 7, 1610, and notes three small stars that he believes to be fixed. After the nights of January 8, 10, and 11, he concludes that three bodies revolve around the planet, as Venus and Mercury revolve around the Sun. On January 13, he sees four at once.

carte.punch: Galileo first mistook Jupiter's moons for fixed stars.
carte.idee: On January 7, 1610, Galileo sees three small stars near Jupiter and takes them to be fixed. Their positions change from one night to the next, and Jupiter has nothing to do with it: on the 11th, he concludes that they revolve around the planet.

quiz.question: What convinces Galileo that the small stars are not fixed stars?
choix: Another astronomer writes to him that he does not see them in the same place
They form a triangle that rotates from one night to the next
Their positions around Jupiter change, and no other star appears near them
Their light is colored, which fixed stars never are
quiz.explication: Galileo records positions that change from one night to the next, along a line that remains Jupiter's, and no other star appears nearby: they are always the same bodies. Such an exchange cannot come from Jupiter itself. The other three reasons do not appear in his account: no letter from a colleague, a line and not a triangle, no color invoked.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Galileo notice on January 8, compared with the previous night?
choix: Two have moved to the east and only one remains in the west, as on January 7
All three are now to the west of Jupiter, closer together and equally spaced
Only one point remains visible, the other two having disappeared that night
They occupy exactly the same position as the night before, with no change at all
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On January 8, the three points are all to the west of Jupiter, close together and equally spaced, whereas the night before two had been to the east. Nothing has disappeared, and the position has not stayed the same.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the first explanation Galileo considers for this change of position?
choix: He fears that Jupiter has moved otherwise than expected, and has passed these stars
He thinks the stars are too small to have a motion of their own
He already suspects that the stars revolve around Jupiter, but wants to check
He believes his instrument distorts the position of Jupiter, not that of the stars
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Galileo first reasons as an astronomer: he fears that Jupiter has moved otherwise than the calculations predicted and has passed these stars by its own motion. The idea of bodies revolving around Jupiter comes only afterward, on January 11.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What does Galileo notice on January 11, in addition to the change of position?
choix: The two visible stars are exactly the same size as on January 10
A fourth star appears that day, to the west of Jupiter
The two stars change color, one turning reddish
The farther of the two visible stars is almost twice as large as the other
quiz_supplementaire.explication: On January 11, the farther of the two visible stars looks almost twice as large as the other, whereas they had seemed equal the night before. The fourth star does not appear until the 13th, and no color is mentioned.
